lessons.title: Anatomy of a Bounded Agent
lessons.summary: Separate model reasoning from the deterministic loop that owns limits and state.

contentBlocks.text: Anatomy of a Bounded Agent

An agent is a controller around a model: it assembles context, asks for a proposed action, validates that action, executes an allowed tool, records the observation, and repeats. Reliability comes from the controller rather than hoping the model stops at the right time.
Production reasoning
items: Represent every turn as an explicit state transition.
Cap steps, elapsed time, tokens, and tool spend.
Terminate on success, policy refusal, or exhausted budget.

contentBlocks.text: The model may propose actions, but deterministic code decides whether an action may run.

lessons.title: Tool Schemas as Contracts
lessons.summary: Design schemas that make invalid actions difficult to express.

contentBlocks.text: Tool Schemas as Contracts

A tool schema is an API contract presented to a probabilistic caller. Narrow enums, required fields, unambiguous units, and explicit error shapes reduce malformed calls and make validation failures teachable to the model.
Production reasoning
items: Use domain types instead of free-form strings.
Describe side effects and permission requirements.
Return stable machine-readable error codes.

contentBlocks.text: A permissive schema shifts ambiguity into runtime, where it becomes expensive and dangerous.

lessons.title: Implement a Step-Bounded Loop
lessons.summary: Code a controller that cannot recurse forever.

contentBlocks.text: Implement a Step-Bounded Loop

A robust loop checks termination before every model call, treats tool errors as observations instead of crashes, and returns a typed terminal reason. This makes runaway behavior testable and lets callers distinguish success from budget exhaustion.
Production reasoning
items: Increment the counter in one deterministic location.
Validate proposed actions before dispatch.
Persist the final reason for evaluation and debugging.

lessons.title: State, Memory, and Event Logs
lessons.summary: Choose state stores by lifetime and correctness needs.

contentBlocks.text: State, Memory, and Event Logs

Working state supports the current task; episodic memory records prior events; semantic memory stores extracted facts. Mixing them into one unbounded transcript raises cost, leaks stale assumptions, and makes deletion or correction nearly impossible.
Production reasoning
items: Keep an append-only event log for auditability.
Build compact working state from relevant events.
Attach provenance and expiry to remembered facts.

contentBlocks.text: Memory is a data product with retention, correction, and access-control requirements—not simply a bigger prompt.

lessons.title: Normalize Tool Results
lessons.summary: Build one result envelope for success, retry, and refusal.

contentBlocks.text: Normalize Tool Results

Agents reason more reliably when every tool returns the same outer shape. A normalized envelope separates a stable status code from user-safe detail, retry guidance, and structured data, so the controller can branch without parsing prose.
Production reasoning
items: Distinguish retryable failures from permanent rejections.
Exclude secrets and raw stack traces from observations.
Preserve a correlation ID across execution.

modules.summary: Add planning, permissions, idempotency, collaboration, and recovery.

lessons.title: Planning Without Pretending
lessons.summary: Use plans as revisable hypotheses, not guaranteed scripts.

contentBlocks.text: Planning Without Pretending

Plans expose dependencies and missing information, but tools return surprises. Reliable agents interleave short planning horizons with observations and re-planning instead of committing to a long chain built on unverified assumptions.
Production reasoning
items: Plan irreversible steps more carefully than reads.
Record assumptions observations can invalidate.
Re-plan after material changes, not every token.

contentBlocks.text: Planning is valuable when it improves control and observability; hidden reasoning is not an operational artifact.

challenge.explanation: Planning is valuable when it improves control and observability; hidden reasoning is not an operational artifact.

lessons.title: Capability-Based Permissions
lessons.summary: Grant the smallest authority needed for one task.

contentBlocks.text: Capability-Based Permissions

Authentication identifies the caller; authorization determines allowed actions; capability tokens can further scope a call to a resource, operation, amount, and expiry. The agent should never infer authority from conversational intent.
Production reasoning
items: Separate read, draft, approve, and execute capabilities.
Require human approval for high-impact transitions.
Re-check authorization inside the tool service.

contentBlocks.text: A prompt cannot grant permission; the service performing the side effect must verify a scoped capability.

lessons.summary: Prevent retries from duplicating side effects.

contentBlocks.text: Make Tool Execution Idempotent
Networks fail after a server commits but before the agent sees the response. An idempotency key lets the service return the original result instead of charging, emailing, or provisioning twice.
Production reasoning
items: Derive the key from a stable logical operation ID.
Store the committed result alongside the key.
Reject key reuse with different arguments.

lessons.title: Multi-Agent Topologies
lessons.summary: Choose specialization only when boundaries are observable.

contentBlocks.text: Multi-Agent Topologies

Multiple agents can isolate contexts and permissions, but every handoff adds latency, cost, and another place to lose intent. Coordinator-worker designs are justified when tasks have distinct tools, access policies, or parallelizable outputs.
Production reasoning
items: Define typed handoff payloads and completion criteria.
Give each worker only the tools it needs.
Trace the parent task across delegated spans.

contentBlocks.text: More agents do not automatically mean more intelligence; topology should follow isolation, parallelism, or expertise needs.

lessons.summary: Implement retries that stop before they become incidents.

contentBlocks.text: Recovery Budgets and Escalation

Retry policy combines attempt count, elapsed time, error class, and side-effect safety. Backoff reduces synchronized load, while escalation preserves the task state an operator needs to continue safely.
Production reasoning
items: Retry only errors classified as transient.
Use jitter to avoid a thundering herd.
Escalate with evidence and remaining choices.

lessons.title: The Evaluation Contract
lessons.summary: Translate a product promise into observable pass and fail criteria.

contentBlocks.text: The Evaluation Contract

An evaluation contract names the population, task, acceptable behavior, forbidden behavior, and release decision the result will inform. Without it, a score can improve while the product becomes worse for important users.
Production reasoning
items: Specify the unit: turn, conversation, task, or outcome.
Separate hard constraints from graded preferences.
Name the release decision and minimum evidence.

contentBlocks.text: A metric is useful only when its boundary matches the product claim.

lessons.title: Representative Evaluation Sets
lessons.summary: Sample cases to expose the distribution you actually serve.

contentBlocks.text: Representative Evaluation Sets

A useful set combines common traffic, high-impact rare cases, known failures, adversarial probes, and time-based holdouts. Random convenience samples often hide the tails that determine operational risk.
Production reasoning
items: Attach slice labels and provenance to every case.
Deduplicate near copies across train and test.
Version cases and record why each was added.

contentBlocks.text: The goal is coverage of consequential behavior, not merely a large row count.

challenge.explanation: The goal is coverage of consequential behavior, not merely a large row count.

contentBlocks.text: Implement Precision, Recall, and F1

Accuracy can look excellent when failures are rare. Precision asks whether positive predictions are trustworthy; recall asks whether actual positives are found; F1 balances them but still needs slice-level interpretation.

items: Guard against zero denominators.
Return component metrics, not only F1.
Keep the classification threshold outside this function.

lessons.title: Designing Model-Judge Evaluations
lessons.summary: Use model graders with rubrics, calibration, and human audits.

contentBlocks.text: Designing Model-Judge Evaluations

A model judge scales evaluation of open-ended outputs but inherits biases, prompt sensitivity, and correlated failures. Strong designs use a concrete rubric, blinded answer order, evidence when appropriate, and human calibration samples.
Production reasoning
items: Measure agreement with expert labels by slice.
Randomize candidate order to detect position bias.
Retain judge rationale for audit, not as truth.

contentBlocks.text: A judge is another measurement instrument; calibrate it before trusting its score.

lessons.summary: Quantify uncertainty without assuming a convenient score distribution.

contentBlocks.text: Bootstrap a Confidence Interval

Bootstrapping repeatedly resamples evaluation cases with replacement and recomputes the statistic. A percentile interval shows how much a mean could move due to finite sampling; paired comparisons reuse sampled indices.
Production reasoning

Resample cases, not token observations.
For comparisons, bootstrap paired score differences.

lessons.title: Slices, Tails, and Adversarial Cases
lessons.summary: Find failures hidden by aggregate averages.

contentBlocks.text: Slices, Tails, and Adversarial Cases

A system can meet its average target while failing a language, device, intent, or safety-sensitive subgroup. Slice evaluation exposes disparity; adversarial cases probe whether the design fails predictably when inputs exploit assumptions.
Production reasoning
items: Pre-register critical slices before seeing results.
Require sample sizes or uncertainty bounds.
Track worst-slice performance beside the global score.

contentBlocks.text: Release decisions should consider users most harmed by error, not only users most common.

lessons.title: Regression Gates That Match Risk
lessons.summary: Use thresholds, deltas, and hard constraints to make release decisions.

contentBlocks.text: Regression Gates That Match Risk

A regression gate should block meaningful harm without freezing development over noise. Combine non-negotiable safety checks, minimum absolute quality, allowed degradation from baseline, and uncertainty-aware review for borderline results.
Production reasoning
items: Pin baseline, dataset, and evaluator versions.
Treat critical safety failures as case-level blockers.
Route ambiguous changes to manual review.

contentBlocks.text: A gate is a policy decision backed by measurement, not a single magic score.

challenge.explanation: A gate is a policy decision backed by measurement, not a single magic score.

lessons.summary: Compare candidates while controlling answer-order bias.

contentBlocks.text: Build a Pairwise Preference Evaluator

Pairwise evaluation is easier than assigning absolute scores, but judges may favor the first or longer answer. Evaluate both orderings, map labels back to stable IDs, and treat inconsistent judgments as review items.
Production reasoning
items: Swap candidate order and map results back.
Represent tie and inconsistency explicitly.
Do not infer a winner when judge calls fail.

lessons.title: Online Experiments for AI Features
lessons.summary: Connect behavioral quality to real user outcomes safely.

contentBlocks.text: Online Experiments for AI Features

Offline evaluations are reproducible but incomplete; online experiments capture adoption, corrections, latency, and downstream impact. Start with guardrails and a small ramp, randomize at a contamination-safe unit, and predefine stopping conditions.
Production reasoning
items: Randomize by user when conversation context carries over.
Log assignment before model execution.
Monitor harm, latency, and cost during the ramp.

contentBlocks.text: An experiment should stop automatically before a promising feature causes unacceptable harm.

lessons.summary: Cluster failures by actionable root cause instead of vague quality labels.

contentBlocks.text: Turn Failures Into Triage Buckets

Evaluation becomes an engineering loop when each failure maps to a layer that can change: data, retrieval, prompt, model capability, tool, policy, or product interaction. A deterministic first pass creates ownership.
Production reasoning
items: Preserve raw evidence and evaluator version.
Allow an unknown bucket rather than forcing certainty.
Count severity and recurrence separately.

lessons.title: Threat-Model the Whole AI System
lessons.summary: Map assets, trust boundaries, attackers, and abuse paths before choosing controls.

contentBlocks.text: Threat-Model the Whole AI System

AI threats cross ordinary application layers: untrusted text enters through users, retrieved documents, tools, or model outputs. A threat model follows data and authority across those boundaries and asks what an attacker gains when any probabilistic assumption fails.
Production reasoning
items: Inventory secrets, private data, money movement, and publishing rights.
Mark every transition from untrusted to privileged context.
Model insider misuse and accidental failure too.

contentBlocks.text: The model is neither the only attack surface nor a security boundary; analyze the complete data-and-tool path.

challenge.instructions: Choose the production-safe answer.

challenge.explanation: The model is neither the only attack surface nor a security boundary; analyze the complete data-and-tool path.

lessons.title: Prompt Injection Is Untrusted Data
lessons.summary: Treat instructions inside content as data unless a trusted controller grants authority.

contentBlocks.text: Prompt Injection Is Untrusted Data

Prompt injection exploits the model's difficulty separating commands from quoted or retrieved content. Delimiters help, but robust defense minimizes tool privilege, labels provenance, validates actions, and keeps policy enforcement deterministic.
Production reasoning
items: Classify each context source by trust and authority.
Never let retrieved text redefine permissions.
Confirm consequential or surprising actions.

contentBlocks.text: No prompt can make arbitrary hostile text safe; containment limits what successful injection can do.

challenge.explanation: No prompt can make arbitrary hostile text safe; containment limits what successful injection can do.
hints: Classify each context source by trust and authority.

contentBlocks.text: Validate Tool Arguments Against Policy
JSON schema validates shape, while policy validation checks meaning: ownership, limits, destinations, and task scope. Tool services enforce both because model-proposed arguments remain untrusted.

items: Fail closed when identity or scope is missing.
Return stable rejection codes without leaking policy detail.
Audit actor, capability, resource, and decision.

lessons.title: Layered Policy Enforcement
lessons.summary: Place controls before, during, and after model execution.

contentBlocks.text: Layered Policy Enforcement

Input checks can reject abuse, the model follows behavioral guidance, tool gateways enforce capabilities, and output validators catch prohibited disclosure. Layering matters because each individual detector has false positives and negatives.
Production reasoning
items: Use deterministic controls for hard invariants.
Log which layer made each allow, block, or escalate decision.
Design a safe fallback when a detector is unavailable.

contentBlocks.text: Defense in depth means independent controls with explicit ownership, not several prompts that fail together.

Verify cited IDs against retrieved evidence.
Redact or block using a documented severity policy.

lessons.title: Secrets, Identity, and Capabilities
lessons.summary: Keep credentials out of prompts and bind every action to verifiable identity.

contentBlocks.text: Secrets, Identity, and Capabilities

Prompts, traces, and transcripts are copied into debugging systems, making them unsafe secret stores. Credentials belong in a secrets manager; a tool gateway exchanges workload identity for short-lived scoped capabilities only when an authorized action is ready.
Production reasoning
items: Use workload identity instead of shared static keys.
Mint credentials with narrow audience, scope, and expiry.
Redact credential-like values before tracing.

lessons.title: AI Supply-Chain Security
lessons.summary: Verify models, datasets, packages, and prompt assets as deployable artifacts.

contentBlocks.text: AI Supply-Chain Security

A compromised model file, tokenizer, dependency, evaluation dataset, or prompt template can bypass source review. Pin versions and digests, scan serialized artifacts, record provenance, and promote only reproducible checked artifacts.
Production reasoning
items: Prefer safe tensor formats over arbitrary deserialization.
Generate a software and model bill of materials.
Separate build-time network access from runtime serving.

contentBlocks.text: AI supply chains include data and model artifacts, not just conventional packages.

lessons.summary: Allocate stricter budgets when identity, action, or anomaly risk rises.

Flat request limits ignore that read-only summaries and privileged bulk actions have different blast radii. A risk-aware limiter combines identity reputation, impact, anomalies, and cost while preserving a hard ceiling.

Use concurrency-safe monotonic windows.

lessons.title: Incident Response for AI Systems
lessons.summary: Preserve evidence and revoke authority before debating model behavior.

contentBlocks.text: Incident Response for AI Systems

An AI incident may involve leaked data, abusive automation, corrupted retrieval, or regression. Response begins by limiting blast radius: disable affected capabilities, freeze versions, preserve restricted traces, and switch to a known safe mode.
Production reasoning
items: Maintain kill switches per tool and tenant.
Record model, prompt, index, policy, and evaluator versions.
Separate communication facts from speculative root cause.

contentBlocks.text: Fast rollback requires every behavior-affecting artifact to be versioned and independently deployable.

Red teaming becomes durable when attacks encode goals, entry channels, expected controls, and severity. The harness distinguishes model refusal from end-to-end containment: an injection can succeed linguistically while the tool gateway still prevents harm.

Assert textual behavior and side-effect absence.
Add confirmed incidents as permanent regression cases.
